content:
An activity diary is a simple record of what you do each day and how your pain and energy feel. If you live with arthritis and frailty, it can show patterns that are hard to notice otherwise, such as doing a lot on a good day and then needing several days to recover. This is often called boom and bust.

This guide explains how to keep a diary, what to look for, and how to use it to pace activity and set small goals. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

Why keep a diary

Memory is not always reliable for pain and tiredness. A written record helps you see which activities help and which make things worse, and gives your GP, physiotherapist or occupational therapist clear information. Pacing, which means balancing activity and rest, is a recognised way to manage fatigue and long-term pain.

How to keep it

  • Use a notebook, a printed table or a phone note, whichever is easiest for your hands.
  • Split each day into morning, afternoon and evening.
  • Write down the main activities and roughly how long each took.
  • Score pain and energy from 0 to 10 at the end of each part of the day.
  • Note sleep, rests, medicines taken and anything unusual, such as a flare or a bad night.
  • Keep it going for one to two weeks before drawing conclusions.

What to look for

  • Boom and bust: a busy day followed by one or more days of high pain or exhaustion.
  • Time of day: whether mornings are stiffest or evenings most tiring.
  • Triggers: particular tasks, such as hoovering or shopping, that are always followed by pain.
  • Too little activity: long stretches sitting, which can lead to stiffness and weaker muscles.

Turning it into a plan

  • Break big tasks into smaller parts with rests in between.
  • Spread demanding jobs across the week.
  • Find a baseline: the amount of an activity you can do on a bad day as well as a good one.
  • Increase slowly, by a small amount each week, if things stay steady.
  • Plan rests before you are exhausted, not after.

Setting tiny goals

Small, specific goals are easier to keep, such as "walk to the end of the garden twice a day" or "stand to make a cup of tea each morning". Write the goal in the diary and tick it off. If you have a setback, go back to a level you could manage and build up again. Setbacks are common and do not mean you have failed.

Sharing it

  • Take the diary to GP, physiotherapy or rheumatology appointments.
  • A carer or family member can help fill it in if writing is painful.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

How long should I keep it?

One to two weeks is usually enough to see patterns. You can restart it after a change, such as a new medicine or a flare.

Is resting always safer?

No. Too much rest can lead to stiffness and weaker muscles. The aim is a steady balance.

What if writing hurts my hands?

Use a voice note, a phone app, or ask someone to write it for you.
